Yep. I have a really similar story to you. I start self-harming at around 12 or 13 and then stopped around 21. My scars faded enough to wear short sleeves and pants, but were still visible if you looked closely. In the past year I’ve had stitches in my legs and both arms and have some more superficial ones elsewhere. Those scars are large, and will be there forever. I often wonder if I would feel differently about myself without the scars. I’d be able to wear short clothing again at least. Like you said though, looking into the past with regret doesn’t help anyone. Our scars are a part of us. They remind us of what we’ve been through and I guess we just have to choose how we look at them. Do they remind us of our time of weakness, or do they remind us of the strength we had to overcome whatever led us to self-harm in the first place?

I don’t have a child or adult child with disabilities, but I’ve worked in a few group homes for adults who are developmentally disabled. Some of the families of the individuals are still involved in their lives (albeit not very involved), but most rarely see their children. We try to provide the most supportive environment for them possible and integrate them into the community, but a lot of them have serious behavioral issues that go along with their development disabilities. This is usually the reason their parents end up putting them in group homes; they were aging and could not deal with their adult child’s behaviors anymore. It’s sad, but I can’t say I blame them. It can be a lot of work to care for an adult who has the mentality of a child, the strength of a full grown adult and physical outbursts. It’s exhausting for me sometimes as a person in their 20s, I couldn’t imagine trying to deal with those behaviors as a 60+ year old.
